name: Streaming lakehouse
description: A streaming lakehouse replaces nightly batch loads with continuous ones: a stream processor consumes the event log and commits micro-batches into open-format tables every minute or two, refining bronze to silver to gold as data flows. Consumers query ordinary lakehouse tables — same SQL, same BI tools — but the answers are minutes old instead of a day old. It unifies the kappa pipeline and the medallion lakehouse into one system: one storage layer, one table format, both streaming freshness and full history for batch reprocessing. The cost is operational: checkpointing, exactly-once commit alignment, and relentless compaction.
when_to_use: Dashboards and downstream systems need minutes-level freshness, but sub-second serving stores would be overkill.
You already run a lakehouse and a separate streaming pipeline, and maintaining two storage layers with two semantics is the pain.
History matters: unlike a pure stream, every event lands in queryable tables, so backfills and reprocessing use the same data.
ML features and BI aggregates should come from the same continuously updated tables.
when_not_to_use: Daily batch freshness satisfies every consumer — a scheduled medallion lakehouse (3) is dramatically simpler to operate.
You need sub-second query-to-event latency — that is a real-time OLAP serving problem (8), not a lakehouse one.
The team has no streaming operations experience; checkpoint recovery and commit tuning are unforgiving on-call material.
Event volumes are trivial — a micro-batch every five minutes through the ordinary batch path costs far less complexity.

hot_spots.title: Small files
hot_spots.detail: Continuous commits without aggressive compaction litter the lake with tiny files and slow every reader within weeks.

hot_spots.title: Exactly-once boundaries
hot_spots.detail: Processor checkpoints and table commits must align — a mismatch after failure recovery duplicates or drops rows silently.

hot_spots.title: Late and out-of-order data
hot_spots.detail: Watermarks decide when windows close; events arriving later than the watermark quietly never reach gold aggregates.

hot_spots.title: Backfill collisions
hot_spots.detail: Reprocessing history through the live pipeline competes with real-time flow and can rewrite tables consumers are reading.

evolution.reason: Scale streaming tables across domains with product ownership once multiple teams build on them.

stages.name: Event log
stages.role: Durable, replayable buffer decoupling producers from the lakehouse
stages.rationale: Kafka is the interoperability standard with the deepest connector and processor ecosystem; Redpanda is wire-compatible with less operational surface, and the cloud logs trade control for zero ops.

stages.name: Stream processor
stages.role: Consumes the log and commits micro-batches into tables with exactly-once semantics
stages.rationale: Flink's checkpointing and Iceberg sink give true exactly-once table commits with event-time watermarks; Structured Streaming is the natural pick on Spark-centric platforms.

stages.name: Lake storage + format
stages.role: Open-format tables receiving continuous commits while staying batch-queryable
stages.rationale: Iceberg's snapshot isolation makes concurrent streaming writes and analytical reads safe; Delta is the equivalent inside Databricks, Hudi shines for upsert-heavy streams.

stages.name: Catalog
stages.role: Registers every commit so readers always see a consistent snapshot
stages.rationale: A REST catalog keeps the streaming writer and every query engine agreeing on the latest snapshot; Nessie adds branch-based deploys for pipeline changes.

stages.name: Table maintenance
stages.role: Continuous compaction and snapshot expiry countering small-file buildup
stages.rationale: Streaming commits make compaction load-bearing, not optional — scheduled Spark rewrite jobs keep file sizes healthy and reads fast.

stages.name: Serving + BI
stages.role: Minutes-fresh SQL over gold tables for dashboards and features
stages.rationale: Trino queries the latest snapshot directly with no copy; ClickHouse enters only when dashboard latency requirements outgrow lakehouse scans.
